bib.title: Branch-Solve-Merge Improves Large Language Model Evaluation and Generation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Branch-Solve-Merge Improves Large Language Model Evaluation and Generation", Swarnadeep Saha, Omer Levy, Asli Celikyilmaz, Mohit Bansal, Jason Weston, Xian Li (UNC Chapel Hill and Meta). arXiv:2310.15123v2, 7 Jun 2024. The PDF carries no venue line, so treat it as a preprint (the Oct 2023 first version dates it; the filename says 2023).
COVERAGE: 76,531 of 76,531 chars read, 19 of 19 pages, in three extraction passes. That includes the appendices, tables 7-11, figures 2-7 and the algorithm. The references were skimmed for origins. Extraction is clean. There are no embedded instructions.

NOTE CONTEXT: Note 06 (line 55) already has two chain examples (MathPrompter, SymbCoT). It has no mention of BSM, branch/solve/merge, or parallel decomposition. BSM is a new shape for it: fan-out into parallel sub-tasks and then merge, a variant of sectioning/parallelization. It is not a sequential chain.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. BSM is a fixed three-prompt program. A branch prompt has the LLM itself plan k parallel sub-tasks, a solve prompt handles each independently, and a merge prompt fuses the results.
 number: none (a design claim)
 setup: all modules are zero-shot prompts to the same base LLM. The LLM decides both the sub-problems and the branching factor.
 quote: "the LLM itself decides (generates) the sub-problems and the corresponding branching factor."
 where: p.3 (Sec 3.1); the abstract says "plan a decomposition of the task into multiple parallel sub-tasks, independently solve them, and fuse the solutions"

2. Branching beats sampling the same problem several times at similar compute. Self-consistency is a special case of BSM (same problem sampled k times, merged by majority vote).
 number: Agreement 0.55 for BSM vs 0.52 for Self-Consistency, 0.43 for Plan&Solve, 0.43/0.45 for zero-shot relative/absolute. Position bias (PB) 17.33 vs 35.66 for SC. Length bias (LB) 39.09 vs 48.12.
 setup: MT-Bench "writing" category, 300 response pairs, LLaMA-2-70B-chat, greedy decoding. Self-consistency samples at temperature 0.7 with the same number of generations as BSM's branching factor.
 quote: "both approaches leverage similar amounts of compute in generating multiple solutions – but branching and solving the differing sub-problems provides superior results to solving the same problem multiple times."
 Table 1 row: "BSM 0.55 17.33 39.09 0.60 14.66 39.46 0.50 20.00 39.13"
 where: p.5, Table 1

3. Plan&Solve (plan, then solve everything in one call) is the ablation for independent solving. BSM's gain over it is up to 12% absolute, and Plan&Solve is no better than zero-shot.
 number: up to 12% absolute over Plan&Solve (overall agreement 0.43 vs 0.55)
 setup: as in claim 2.
 quote: "it obtains up to 12% absolute improvement over Plan&Solve, which specifically shows the utility of branching into and solving independent sub-problems."
 where: p.5

4. Headline: BSM raises LLM-human agreement by up to 26% absolute and cuts position bias by up to 50%. It lets LLaMA-2-70B-chat match or beat GPT-4 on several MT-Bench domains.
 number: STEM agreement 0.46 to 0.72 (+26) vs GPT-4 0.72. Writing PB 51.66 to 17.33 (relative zero-shot to BSM).
 setup: LLaMA-2-70B-chat. BSM beats zero-shot in every domain table. Matches or approaches GPT-4 on 3 of 4 domains in Table 5 (Extraction is far below: 0.55 vs 0.71).
 quote: "BSM improves LLM-human agreement by up to absolute 26% and even matches or outperforms GPT-4 on many domains."
 Table 5 STEM: "BSM (w/ LLaMA-2-70B-c) 0.72 10.33 44.68 ... GPT-4 0.72 13.66 46.80"
 where: p.2 intro, p.6 Table 5, p.9 App A.2

5. BSM improves every base model, with the smallest gain on the strongest. The biggest gain is on turn-2 (long-context) questions.
 number: Writing agreement: LLaMA-2-7B 0.39 to 0.41; Vicuna-33B 0.51 to 0.56; LLaMA-2-70B 0.43 to 0.55; GPT-4 0.59 to 0.62. Turn-2 gains up to 16%.
 setup: MT-Bench writing, zero-shot vs BSM, same base model.
 quote: "Even though zero-shot GPT-4 is the state-of-the-art LLM-based evaluator, applying BSM obtains a further improvement of 3%."
 Table 3 caption: "BSM improves agreement for all models and reduces biases for all models except GPT-4."
 where: p.6 Table 3

6. Reference-based categories. BSM beats zero-shot, and on math beats GPT-4 on all metrics.
 number: Coding 0.47 to 0.61 (PB 52.33 to 25.66). Reasoning 0.47 to 0.57. Math 0.52 to 0.64 (PB 17.66), vs GPT-4 0.62 (PB 19.00).
 setup: reference answers are generated once by GPT-4 and appended to the prompt. The paper states that curating these answers once is a key assumption.
 quote: "On Math, it even outperforms the state-of-the-art GPT-4 evaluator, outperforming on all metrics."
 where: p.6 Table 4

7. Constrained story generation (10 concepts, 100 samples): BSM raises constraint satisfaction and wins on coherence.
 number: All Present (AP) 28.0 vs 22.0 zero-shot on 70B. 23.0 vs 15.0 on 7B. Missing Concepts (MC) 14.7 vs 27.2 on 70B. GPT-4 judge prefers BSM stories 93% of the time (vs zero-shot, 70B).
 setup: CommonGen-hard-style task from Self-Refine data, LLaMA-2-7B-chat and 70B-chat, greedy decoding. Branch splits the concepts into two groups and picks a shared topic. Solve writes one story per group. Merge fuses the two stories. Pairwise GPT-4 judging is run twice with order swapped, and a verdict counts only if consistent.
 quote: "stories generated by BSM are preferred a substantial 93% of the time by GPT-4."
 Table 6: "BSM 23.0 15.5 28.0 14.7"
 where: p.7

8. Even with BSM the task is mostly unsolved: 72% of stories still miss a concept. Most omissions occur inside solve, not merge.
 number: 72% of 70B BSM stories miss at least one concept (AP 28.0 means 72%). Of those, 60 points are omissions at solve and 12 at merge.
 setup: LLaMA-2-70B-chat. The 60% and 12% are shares of all stories (they sum to 72%).
 quote: "out of 72% of the BSM stories (with LLaMA-2-70B-chat) where at least one concept is missing, a significant 60% of these belong to the first category (i.e., concept omission in the ‘solve’ module) versus only 12% belong to the second category"
 Model scale had little effect: "the scale of the model has little impact on constraint satisfaction."
 where: p.7 and App B, p.10

9. Branching factor (BF): agreement saturates around 4 branches, position bias keeps falling as branches are added.
 number: BF 2/3/4/5 agreement 0.50/0.52/0.53/0.52. PB 22/19/19/12.
 setup: 100 writing samples, LLaMA-2-70B-chat. The prompt caps the plan at "up to five factors".
 quote: "We observe highest agreement at a branching factor of 4, after which the result mostly saturates."
 where: App A.2, Table 10, p.10

10. Adding self-consistency inside each branch (BSM+SC, 5 samples at temperature 0.7 per branch) gives no agreement gain and only a small bias gain. Branches are already granular.
 number: agreement 0.55 for both. PB 17.33 to 15.33.
 setup: LLaMA-2-70B-chat, writing.
 quote: "While agreement scores do not improve further, we observe a 2% reduction in position bias."
 where: p.9, Table 8

11. The scale used in the solve prompt matters little. 1-5 gives agreement 0.52 and PB 12.00. 1-10 gives 0.50 and PB 18.00. Position bias rises slightly on the 1-10 scale.
 setup: 100 writing samples, 70B.
 where: App A.2, Table 11

12. Self-enhancement check: GPT-4 as judge on pairs where GPT-4 wrote one response.
 number: agreement 0.51 to 0.54 (3 points). PB goes 6.33 to 7.33 and LB 36.36 to 34.54.
 quote: "We observe a 3% better correlation with humans, suggesting that BSM improves evaluation even when the LLM judges its own outputs."
 caveat: the paper says this "does not necessarily compute whether an evaluator has less SB".
 where: p.5, Table 2

13. Position bias is handled by running the whole program twice with response order swapped. Answer A or B only if both runs agree, otherwise tie. All baselines get the same treatment.
 number: none (2 runs per judgment)
 quote: "The final judgment is either ‘A’ or ‘B’ if and only if the judgement is consistent for both orders, otherwise it is a ‘tie’."
 where: p.4 (Sec 3.2), Algorithm 1 p.12

14. Merge for evaluation is a plain sum of per-branch scores, not an LLM call. A neural merge exists but was not used in the reported results.
 quote: "we find that the non-neural merge of summing up the criterion-wise evaluations is simple and works well in practice, hence all our experimental results are reported with that method."
 where: p.9 (App A.1)

15. Branches adapt by domain from one fixed branch prompt, with no human-written plans. Writing branches: Clarity, Relevance, Creativity, Accuracy. Coding branches: Efficiency, Correctness, Code Readability, Time Efficiency.
 quote: "We observe almost no overlap between the branch names of coding questions and writing questions."
 where: p.6

LIMITS
- Authors concede (p.7): safety, toxicity and bias are not evaluated. Length bias is hard to isolate, since humans also prefer longer answers. Recursive or multi-level BSM is not explored because of cost. Efficiency gains from parallelism are not measured: "in this work, we instead focused on improving the task performance."
- No cost figure is given. BSM needs k solve calls plus a branch call, and doubles that for the order-swapped second run. Compute is matched only against self-consistency, and only on the number of generations. Wall-clock, tokens and dollars are not reported.
- The main table is the single "writing" category. Per-domain samples are about 300 pairs (the 100-sample ablations are smaller). No confidence intervals or seeds are reported, and greedy decoding is used throughout.
- Position bias is lower partly because the tie rule makes disagreement into ties. This applies to the baselines too.
- Merge for evaluation is a sum, so "merge" there is a non-LLM aggregator.
- The story task has 100 samples. The judge is GPT-4 alone, and BSM stories are fused from two paragraphs, which may favour them.
- BSM gains little on GPT-4 (+3 points), and bias gets no better for GPT-4 (Table 3 caption).
- Models are 2023-era (LLaMA-2, Vicuna, GPT-4), so absolute numbers are dated.
- Reference-based evaluation relies on GPT-4 reference answers.
- Dated: the paper contrasts itself with sequential-decomposition prompting for reasoning (least-to-most, plan-and-solve), noting that "most of these works typically focus on reasoning problems ... that benefit from sequential decompositions."

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Schlag et al., 2023 (LLM programs) and Dohan et al., 2022 (language model cascades).
- Wang et al., 2022 (self-consistency).
- Wang et al., 2023a (plan-and-solve).
- Zhou et al., 2022 (least-to-most) and Khot et al., 2022 (decomposed prompting).
- Ning et al., 2023 (skeleton-of-thought, parallel decoding).
- Besta et al., 2023 and Lei et al., 2023 (graph of thoughts).
- Zheng et al., 2023 (MT-Bench and LLM-as-judge).
- Lin et al., 2020 (CommonGen) and Madaan et al., 2023 (Self-Refine, the hard variant).
- Liu et al., 2023 (G-Eval, hand-designed evaluation plans).

CODE (verbatim, Fig 4/6, p.12-13)
- Branch prompt, evaluation: "...Your task is to propose an evaluation plan that can be executed to compare the two responses. The evaluation plan should consist of a list of up to five factors that one should consider such as helpfulness, relevance, accuracy, etc. In each line, write an evaluation criterion along with a short descrition of how we should evaluate that criterion."
- Solve prompt: "...evaluate and score the quality of the responses based on a single evaluation criterion displayed below. Make sure to evaluate only based on the criterion specified and none other. In the first line, provide a score between 1 to 5 for Assistant A's response. In the second line, provide a score between 1 to 5 for Assistant B's response."
- Story branch prompt: "...first propose a story topic and then divide the concepts into two groups such that the story generated from each group of concepts can be combined together to form a longer story. Make sure that you do not leave out any concepts."
- Story merge prompt: "Given two groups of concepts and two stories containing those concepts, combine the two stories into a concise and coherent story consisting of a single paragraph. Make sure that the combined story does not miss any concept from the two groups."
- Consistency rule (Algorithm 1): "if y(A,B) = A & y(B,A) = B then y ← A ... else y ← tie"

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): BSM pairwise evaluation of two responses to a Hawaii travel-blog prompt with LLaMA-2-70B-chat. Branch makes criteria (Relevance, Clarity, Accuracy, Originality), each solved with a 1-5 score per response, then merged into a verdict. It is the clearest picture of the fan-out and merge shape and the best candidate for the note.
- Fig 3 (p.12): story generation. 10 concepts are split into two groups plus a topic, one story is written per group, and the two are merged. A compact worked example of constraint splitting.
- Fig 2 (p.11): generated branches for a turn-2 writing question and a coding question. It shows the plan adapting to the task.
- Fig 4-6: the prompts (see CODE).
- Table 1 and Table 10 are the quantitative pieces worth a small table.

PROBLEMS: none. Text extraction was clean, with only minor ligature or spacing artifacts. The PDF contained no instructions aimed at the reader.
